analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. prescription drug prices at the median price charged in eleven other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its introduction: it was referred to the Senate health committee and died there with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Secretary of Health and Human Services to set a yearly reference price for every prescription drug, based mainly on the median price charged in eleven other wealthy countries such as Japan, Germany, France, and Canada. No drug sold under Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA care, or other federal programs could be priced above that cap. Manufacturers would also have to offer the same price to uninsured people and to people with private insurance, and companies that charged more would owe a civil penalty of five times the overcharge, with the money going to NIH for drug research.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who buy prescription drugs: patients in Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA care, and Indian Health programs, plus uninsured people and anyone with private insurance, who would all be guaranteed the reference price — a cap set at the median price charged in eleven other advanced countries. Employers and taxpayers would also save as health program and private-plan drug spending fell.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the retail list price of every prescription drug at a reference price, generally the median price charged in eleven other advanced countries including Japan, Germany, France, and Canada.
Applies the cap across Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA care, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and Indian Health Service programs.
Requires manufacturers to offer the same reference price to people without insurance and to people with private coverage, so the cap reaches almost everyone who buys drugs.

Imposes a civil penalty on manufacturers who overcharge — five times the difference between what they collected and what they should have — and sends the penalty money to the National Institutes of Health for drug research.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and generic drug manufacturers, whose U.S. revenues would drop to match the median prices charged in peer countries, and by extension their shareholders. Some of the industry's revenue funds research and development, so a price cap could mean less investment in future drugs — an objection its opponents raised to similar proposals.

drawbacks.text: Capping U.S. prices at the median of eleven other wealthy countries would cut deeply into pharmaceutical revenues, which manufacturers warn could mean less investment in new drug development.

For drugs not available in at least three reference countries, the price would be set by the HHS Secretary's own judgment of a drug's value, which gives a government official wide discretion over what new medicines can charge.
The penalty for overcharging is calculated only on federal program sales, so enforcement pressure depends heavily on those sales volumes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—capping what Americans pay for drugs at prices other wealthy countries pay—would have been large for patients, insurers, and taxpayers. The cost is that cutting U.S. prices toward international levels could reduce revenue that funds pharmaceutical research, though the bill redirected any penalty revenue into NIH research. The bigger practical weakness was political: the bill never attracted a single cosponsor and never received a hearing or vote, so its design was never tested or debated in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's health committee never took it up, so the bill sat after introduction until the two-year session ended and it expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 26, 2019 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no companion action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
Not a single senator signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill without a second name.

The bill's core mechanism was to cap drug list prices at the median price in eleven reference countries and extend that cap to uninsured and privately insured people, with civil penalties for noncompliance.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who kept the current pricing system with no cap on U.S. drug prices. American patients and federal health programs gained nothing from the bill's failure.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturer industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed international reference-pricing proposals generally during this period; no group-specific action on this bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; it attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so its level of support within the Senate cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would cap their U.S. list prices at the median of prices in eleven other wealthy countries and penalize overcharging at five times the excess amount, directly cutting the revenue that comes from the United States being the world's highest-price market.
Reference prices apply to generics and other non-brand drugs as well, capping what they can charge under federal programs.

industries.industry: Private health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Insurers would benefit because the cap applies to what their members pay, reducing claims costs; the bill does not restructure their role.
Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, and VA prescription spending would fall, easing federal and state budgets; any penalty revenue is routed to NIH research rather than back to the Treasury.
